content:
A flare of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis can knock you off your feet for days, and in later life a week mostly in a chair or bed can cost strength that is slow to win back. Get through it with a plan: contact your rheumatology advice line early if the flare is not settling, keep taking your usual medicines unless your team tells you otherwise, use the pain relief and flare plan you have agreed, and keep moving a little every hour so you do not stiffen and weaken. Line up help with meals and shopping, keep your phone with you, and get urgent help for a fever, sudden confusion or one hot, very swollen joint. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is for people with rheumatoid arthritis or another inflammatory arthritis, and the people who help them, who want a practical plan for a bad flare week in later life. If you are not sure it is a flare at all, read is it a flare or something else? first. For flares in general, including osteoarthritis, see what to do in an arthritis flare.

Before the next flare: get your plan ready

Flares are easier to manage when the decisions are made on a good day. Ask your rheumatology team or GP to help you write a short flare plan and keep it on the fridge or in your phone:

  • The rheumatology advice line number, its opening hours and what to do out of hours. NICE NG100 says people with rheumatoid arthritis should have rapid access to specialist care when they flare.
  • Which pain relief is safe for you to use during a flare, agreed with your GP, team or pharmacist, especially if you have kidney, stomach or heart problems.
  • Whether your team would ever offer a steroid tablet or injection for a flare, and how you would ask for it. Do not start, restart or increase steroids on your own.
  • Who can help with shopping, meals, pets and lifts for a few days, and their numbers.
  • A list of your medicines, or your NHS App, so anyone who helps can see it.

Our printable flare action plan gives you a template to fill in.

Days 1 and 2: calm things down

  • Keep taking your usual arthritis medicines, including methotrexate, other DMARDs and biologics, unless your team has told you to pause them. Stopping them yourself can make the flare worse.
  • Use your agreed flare treatments: pain relief as directed on the label or by your pharmacist, and warmth or cold packs if they help (wrapped in a towel, for short spells, never on numb skin or in bed while asleep).
  • Rest in short spells, not all day. Rest the worst joints, for example with a splint your therapist has given you, but keep the rest of you moving.
  • Ring the advice line if the flare is severe, involves new joints or is no better after a couple of days. Write down which joints are affected, how long morning stiffness lasts and what you have taken.

Keep moving a little every hour

In later life, a few days with very little movement can leave muscles noticeably weaker and make getting up, walking and the stairs harder. You do not need to exercise hard during a flare. Aim for small, gentle movement through the day:

  • Each hour you are awake, stand up if you safely can and walk to another room, or do a few sit-to-stands from a firm chair.
  • Move each joint gently through a comfortable range: open and close the hands, circle the wrists and ankles, lift the arms as far as is comfortable.
  • Do seated exercises on the days you cannot stand for long. Our guide to seated exercise with rheumatoid arthritis explains what to do on flare days and good days.
  • Spread tasks across the day and stop before you are exhausted. See RA fatigue in later life for pacing.

Food, drink and sleep

  • Keep easy food in: ready meals, tins with ring pulls, yoghurts, bread, eggs, soup. Try to have some protein at each meal to help protect your muscles.
  • Keep drinking through the day, even if getting to the toilet is hard. Not drinking enough can make you dizzy and confused and adds to the risk of falls.
  • Pain and steroids can both disturb sleep. Keep a regular bedtime, and ask your GP or team if sleep stays poor after the flare.

Staying safe at home

Stiff, painful joints make falls more likely, especially first thing in the morning and at night.

  • Keep your phone or alarm on you, not across the room.
  • Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing, and have a light you can reach.
  • Move things you use every day to between waist and shoulder height.
  • If you are struggling to wash, dress or get to the toilet, tell your GP. You can also ask your council for a free care needs assessment, which can lead to equipment or short-term help at home.

Medicines and infections during a flare

Many treatments for inflammatory arthritis lower your ability to fight infection, and an infection can also set off a flare or feel like one.

  • If you take methotrexate, another DMARD or a biologic and get signs of an infection, such as a high temperature, shivering, a sore throat or a cough that will not go away, contact your GP, team or NHS 111 the same day. Ask them whether to keep taking your medicines; do not decide on your own.
  • If you take steroid tablets every day, carry your steroid card and tell anyone treating you. Your team will tell you what to do if you are ill.
  • If you are offered ibuprofen or another anti-inflammatory, check first with a pharmacist. The NHS advises caution with these medicines in older people and in people with kidney, heart or stomach problems.

When to get help straight away

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if someone is suddenly confused or very drowsy, has signs of sepsis (for example very cold or blotchy skin, very fast breathing or being hard to wake), or has had a fall and may have broken a bone.
  • Get a same-day GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for one joint that is suddenly hot, swollen and much more painful than the others, especially with a temperature, because it could be a joint infection; for a fever while on DMARDs or biologics; or if you cannot get up, eat or drink.
  • Ring the rheumatology advice line during opening hours if the flare is not settling with your plan.

After the flare: get your strength back

When the pain settles, build back up over a week or two: a little more walking each day, back to your usual exercises, and back to the jobs you dropped. Our guide to getting your strength back after a flare has a step-by-step plan.

Tell your team about the flare at your next review. If flares are happening often, or each one takes longer to recover from, your treatment may need changing. NICE NG100 recommends regular reviews that aim to keep disease activity low. Our guide to RA monitoring in later life explains what is checked.

For family and carers

Help with the practical things (meals, shopping, prescriptions, pets) but encourage the person to keep doing the small movements they can. Watch for changes that suggest something other than a flare, such as new confusion, not eating or drinking, or a fever, and act on them.

Common questions

Should I stay in bed during a flare?

Short rests help, but staying in bed for days weakens muscles quickly in later life. Get up and move a little every hour if you safely can.

Can I stop my methotrexate during a flare?

No. Do not stop or change it yourself. If you have an infection or feel unwell, contact your team, GP or NHS 111 and ask what to do.

How long does a flare last?

It varies from a few days to a few weeks. If it is not settling with your plan, ring your advice line rather than waiting for your next appointment.
